title: Plans, weather and leisure
objectives: I can talk about future plans with ir plus an infinitive.
I can describe the weather and name the seasons.
I can invite someone, and accept or decline an invitation politely.
I can use poder, querer, saber, precisar and dever with an infinitive and talk about hobbies.
I can explain why words such as céu, sábado, futebol and amanhã are written and pronounced as they are.

vocabulary.note: One word covers both meanings and the sentence decides which: como está o tempo? asks about the weather, and eu não tenho tempo is about time. The m of tempo ends its syllable before p, so it only nasalizes the e: TEM-poo, with the e through the nose.

example.en: How is the weather today?

vocabulary.note: A written l at the end of a syllable is said like the w at the end of English 'now'. So sol is one syllable, an open o followed by that w: SOHW.

example.en: It is sunny today.

vocabulary.note: Ch is the sound of English 'sh': SHOO-vuh. The related verb is chover, to rain.

example.en: Tomorrow there will be rain.

vocabulary.note: The n ends the syllable before t, so it nasalizes the e: VEN-too, with the e through the nose.

example.en: It is very windy today.

vocabulary.note: Formed from the verb nublar, to cloud over. The ending -ado turns a verb into an adjective, the way English -ed does in 'clouded'.

example.en: The sky is cloudy.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the last syllable, ca-LOR. A word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent is written. Masculine, so muito calor.

example.en: It is very hot in the summer.

vocabulary.note: The ending io may be said as one quick syllable or as two; the stress is on fri either way. The r after f is a tap. As an adjective it is frio, fria: está frio.

example.en: It is cold in the winter.

vocabulary.note: The ending ão is a nasal diphthong, stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde needs no other accent: ve-RÃO. The single r between vowels is a tap. In Brazil summer runs from December to March.

example.pt: No verão a gente vai à praia.
example.en: In summer we go to the beach.
example.literal: In-the summer the-people goes to-the beach.

vocabulary.note: The n ends the first syllable before v, so it nasalizes the i: in-VER-noo, with the first i through the nose.

example.pt: O inverno no Sul é frio.
example.en: Winter in the South is cold.

vocabulary.note: Nh is one sound, like 'ny' in canyon. The tilde nasalizes the a and also marks the stress, which falls on the last syllable: a-ma-NHÃ. The word contains manhã, morning.

example.en: Tomorrow I'm going to travel.

vocabulary.note: Fim ends in im, a nasal i: the lips do not close at the end. De is said like jee, because d before the sound i is said like English j. You also hear o final de semana.

example.pt: O que você vai fazer no fim de semana?
example.en: What are you going to do on the weekend?
example.literal: What you go to-do in-the end of week?

vocabulary.note: Ai is a diphthong, so the word is PRAI-a. The r after p is a tap. Feminine, so you say à praia and na praia.

example.pt: Eu quero ir à praia no domingo.
example.en: I want to go to the beach on Sunday.

vocabulary.note: The English word football respelled with Portuguese sounds. It is said fu-chee-BOHW: the final l is said w, and the unstressed e before the stressed syllable is said i in most Brazilian accents, so the t before it becomes ch. It ends in l, so the stress is on the last syllable and no accent is written.

example.pt: Meu pai joga futebol com os amigos.
example.en: My father plays soccer with his friends.
example.literal: My father plays soccer with the friends.

vocabulary.note: Ch is sh and rr is the strong h sound: shoo-HAS-koo. The s ends the syllable, so it is said s or sh depending on the region. The ending o gives default stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent.

example.pt: A gente faz um churrasco no domingo.
example.en: We have a barbecue on Sunday.
example.literal: The-people makes a barbecue on-the Sunday.

vocabulary.note: A false friend: it names a gym, not an academy. Stressed on the second to last syllable, a-ca-de-MI-a, which is the default for a word ending in a, so no accent is written. Compare comédia in the spelling note.

example.pt: Eu vou à academia de manhã.
example.en: I go to the gym in the morning.
example.literal: I go to-the academy of morning.

vocabulary.note: Also the art form, the movies. Ir ao cinema is the normal way to say go to the movies. The c before i is said s: si-NE-ma.

example.pt: Que tal cinema hoje à noite?
example.en: How about the movies tonight?
example.literal: What such cinema today at-the night?

vocabulary.note: The s ends the first syllable (FES-ta), so it is said s or sh by region. The e is open, but nothing in the spelling says so; learn it with the word.

example.en: The party is on Saturday.

vocabulary.note: J is always the sound of the s in 'measure'. Stressed on the last syllable, vi-a-JAR, which is the default for a word ending in r, so no accent. The noun is a viagem, the trip.

example.en: I'm going to travel in July.

vocabulary.note: Used for games and sports: jogar futebol. It also means to throw, as in jogar fora, to throw away. G before a is the hard sound, as in go.

example.en: We are going to play soccer.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the last syllable, na-DAR, which is the default for a word ending in r, so no accent. The d here is before the vowel a, so it is an ordinary d; it would be said j only before the sound i.

example.en: I don't know how to swim.

vocabulary.note: Ficar means to stay or remain here, and also to be located or to become. Em casa has no article, like para casa. The s of casa is between vowels, so it is said z.

example.pt: Hoje eu vou ficar em casa.
example.en: Today I'm going to stay home.
example.literal: Today I go to-stay in house.

vocabulary.note: Also may, for permission: posso entrar? In the eu form the stem pod- becomes poss-, written with ss to keep the s sound between vowels. Pode is said PÓ-jee, with an open o and d before the final e said like j. There is also a past form pôde, whose circumflex shows a closed o and tells the two words apart.

example.en: I can't go today.

vocabulary.en: to know, to know how to
vocabulary.note: Saber is to know a fact or to know how to do something you have learned: eu sei nadar. A different verb, conhecer, covers knowing a person or a place. The eu form sei does not look like the stem at all.

example.en: Do you know how to play soccer?

vocabulary.note: Before a noun it takes de, literally to-need of: preciso de ajuda. Before an infinitive there is no de: preciso estudar. C before i is said s, and the s between two vowels is said z: pre-ci-SAR. It ends in r, so the stress is on the last syllable.

example.en: I need to work tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: The basic meaning is to owe, as in devo dinheiro, I owe money. The sense of duty grew out of owing something. Dever expresses advice or an expected duty, milder than must.

example.en: You should rest.

vocabulary.note: Vamos is the nós form of ir, so an invitation is literally we go, said with rising intonation. Said without the rise it is a call to action, Vamos! Let's go!

example.en: Shall we go to the beach?

vocabulary.note: Que is what and tal is such, so the phrase asks what about something such as this. It is followed by a noun or an infinitive; standard usage does not put a conjugated verb straight after it. The u of que is silent and the l of tal is said w: kee TAHW.

example.pt: Que tal um churrasco no sábado?
example.en: How about a barbecue on Saturday?
example.literal: What such a barbecue on-the Saturday?

vocabulary.note: Informal. Topar means to accept or go along with a plan; its older sense is to bump into something. To accept, use the eu form: topo, or topo, sim.

example.pt: A gente vai ao cinema. Você topa?
example.en: We're going to the movies. Are you up for it?
example.literal: The-people goes to-the cinema. You accept?

vocabulary.note: Said to show sympathy or regret, for instance when someone declines your invitation. Portuguese has no article here: what pity. The same spelling pena also means feather.

example.pt: Você não pode ir? Que pena!
example.en: You can't go? What a pity!
example.literal: You not can go? What pity!

vocabulary.note: A strong yes when you accept an invitation. Com ends in m, so the o is nasal. The c before e is said s, and the z between vowels is said z: com ser-TE-za.

example.en: Of course I'll go!

dialogues.title: Planos para o fim de semana
dialogues.context: Beatriz and her friend Thiago talk about what they are going to do this weekend.

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.pt: Oi, Thiago! O que você vai fazer no fim de semana?
lines.en: Hi, Thiago! What are you going to do on the weekend?
lines.literal: Hi, Thiago! What you go to-do in-the end of week?

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.pt: No sábado eu vou jogar futebol com os amigos. E você?
lines.en: On Saturday I'm going to play soccer with friends. And you?
lines.literal: In-the Saturday I go to-play soccer with the friends. And you?

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.pt: Eu vou ficar em casa. Preciso estudar.
lines.en: I'm going to stay home. I need to study.
lines.literal: I go to-stay in house. I-need to-study.

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.pt: No domingo a gente vai fazer um churrasco. Você topa?
lines.en: On Sunday we're going to have a barbecue. Are you up for it?
lines.literal: In-the Sunday the-people goes to-make a barbecue. You accept?

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.pt: Com certeza! Que horas?
lines.en: Definitely! What time?
lines.literal: With certainty! What hours?

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.pt: Por volta da uma hora.
lines.en: Around one o'clock.
lines.literal: By turn of-the one hour.

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.pt: Posso levar alguma coisa?
lines.en: Can I bring something?
lines.literal: Can-I take some thing?

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.pt: Pode levar um refrigerante.

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.pt: Combinado. Vai ter sol?
lines.en: Deal. Will it be sunny?
lines.literal: Agreed. Goes to-have sun?

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.pt: Vai! Vai fazer calor.
lines.en: It will! It's going to be hot.
lines.literal: Goes! Goes to-make heat.

dialogues.title: Vamos à praia?
dialogues.context: Camila, Diego and Larissa are friends in Rio de Janeiro. Camila wants to go to the beach.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Gente, vamos à praia amanhã?
lines.en: Guys, shall we go to the beach tomorrow?
lines.literal: People, we-go to-the beach tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.pt: Amanhã eu não posso. Preciso trabalhar. Que tal no domingo?
lines.en: I can't tomorrow. I need to work. How about Sunday?
lines.literal: Tomorrow I not can. I-need to-work. What such in-the Sunday?

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: Domingo eu posso. Mas vai fazer calor ou vai chover?
lines.en: I can on Sunday. But will it be hot, or is it going to rain?
lines.literal: Sunday I can. But goes to-make heat or goes to-rain?

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: No celular, domingo tem sol e faz trinta graus.
lines.en: On the phone, Sunday is sunny and thirty degrees.
lines.literal: In-the cellphone, Sunday has sun and makes thirty degrees.

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: Perfeito! Eu vou levar o protetor solar.
lines.en: Perfect! I'm going to bring the sunscreen.
lines.literal: Perfect! I go to-take the protector solar.

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.pt: Eu não sei nadar bem, mas gosto da praia.
lines.en: I don't swim well, but I like the beach.
lines.literal: I not know to-swim well, but I-like of-the beach.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Sem problema! A gente vai de ônibus?
lines.en: No problem! Are we going by bus?
lines.literal: Without problem! The-people goes of bus?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.pt: Vamos de ônibus, eu não tenho carro.

lines.literal: We-go of bus, I not have car.

lines.speaker: Larissa
lines.pt: Então a gente se encontra no ponto às oito.
lines.en: Then we'll meet at the bus stop at eight.
lines.literal: Then the-people self finds in-the stop at-the eight.

dialogues.title: Que pena!
dialogues.context: Ana invites her coworker Rui to the movies, but he has a problem.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Rui, você quer ir ao cinema hoje à noite?
lines.en: Rui, do you want to go to the movies tonight?
lines.literal: Rui, you want to-go to-the cinema today at-the night?

lines.speaker: Rui
lines.pt: Hoje eu não posso. Preciso trabalhar até tarde.
lines.en: I can't today. I need to work late.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Que pena! E amanhã?
lines.en: What a pity! And tomorrow?
lines.literal: What pity! And tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Rui
lines.pt: Amanhã sim. Que filme você quer ver?
lines.en: Tomorrow, yes. What movie do you want to see?
lines.literal: Tomorrow yes. What film you want to-see?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Uma comédia. Vamos às sete?
lines.en: A comedy. Shall we go at seven?
lines.literal: A comedy. We-go at-the seven?

lines.speaker: Rui
lines.pt: Às sete está ótimo. Mas amanhã vai chover.
lines.en: Seven is great. But it's going to rain tomorrow.
lines.literal: At-the seven is great. But tomorrow goes to-rain.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Sem problema. O cinema fica no shopping.
lines.en: No problem. The movie theater is in the mall.
lines.literal: Without problem. The cinema stays in-the shopping.

lines.speaker: Rui
lines.pt: Verdade! Então combinado. A gente se encontra lá.
lines.en: True! Then it's a deal. We'll meet there.
lines.literal: Truth! Then agreed. The-people self finds there.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the new words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every new written pattern in this unit can be worked out from the first three lessons, and this note does that for the words you meet first. The method is the one from the lesson on reading: look for marks (tilde, accent, cedilla); group the letters that work as a unit (ch, nh, lh, rr, ss, qu, and a vowel followed by an m or n that ends its syllable); check the letter after c, g, s, t, d, l and r; weaken the final vowels; then find the stress. Nothing below is a new rule. It is practice with the old ones.

Nasal vowels. A vowel followed by m or n at the end of a syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not said as a consonant: tempo is TEM-poo with the e through the nose, and vento, domingo, trinta, inverno, fim, sem, com and então all work the same way. The tilde does the same job on a and o: amanhã, verão, então. When a word has no other accent, the tilde also marks the stressed syllable. That is why amanhã is a-ma-NHÃ and verão is ve-RÃO with nothing else written: ão and ã at the end of a word are stressed on the last syllable by default.

The letter l at the end of a syllable is said w, like the end of English 'now': sol is SOHW, futebol is fu-chee-BOHW, and tal is TAHW. In filme the l ends the first syllable, so it is FIW-mee. An l at the start of a syllable is an ordinary l, as in calor.

T and d before the sound i. A t or d before an i, or before an e that is said i, becomes ch or j: gente is ZHEN-chee, sete is SEH-chee, tarde is TAR-jee, verdade is ver-DA-jee, dia is JEE-a, and de is jee. In futebol the unstressed e before the stressed syllable is also said i in most Brazilian accents, so the t becomes ch. Names follow the same rule: Thiago is an old spelling with th for t, said CHYA-goo, and the d of Diego is said j.

Digraphs and double letters. Ch is sh (chuva, churrasco, chover). Nh is the ny of canyon (amanhã). Lh is the lli of million (trabalhar). Rr is the strong h sound (churrasco, carro), while a single r between vowels is a tap (verão, hora). Ss is always the s sound (posso, passear), while a single s between two vowels is z (casa, preciso, coisa), as is the letter z itself (certeza). The u of qu is silent before e and i (que, quer, quero, quente), and g before e or i is the s of measure (gente), as is j in every position (viajar, jogar). On its own, h is never said: hoje, hora, Thiago.

Accents follow the default stress rule from the lesson on accents. Céu is one syllable. The diphthong éu is open, and Portuguese writes an acute on a stressed open diphthong at the end of a word (céu, papéis, herói). Sábado, ótimo and comédia are stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending can predict, so the accent is always written, and the quality of the vowel chooses the acute. In comédia the ending ia counts as two syllables, co-MÉ-di-a. Compare academia, a-ca-de-MI-a: the stress is on the second to last syllable, which the ending a already predicts, so nothing is written. Até is a-TÉ: it ends in e and is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default. The grave in à noite, à tarde and às oito records that the preposition a has fused with the article a or as.

The small words of this unit follow the same procedure. Lá (there) and nós (we) are stressed words of one syllable ending in a or o (with or without a final s), and such words always take the acute, which also keeps them apart from unstressed small words (nos, meaning us). Está is es-TÁ: it ends in a but is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default, where esta (this) is ES-ta with no mark. Você is vo-CÊ for the same reason, with a closed e, so the circumflex. Ônibus is Ô-ni-bus, stressed on the third to last syllable, so it is always marked, and the closed o takes the circumflex. É (is) is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it is marked, while e (and) is an unstressed small word. Não, são and vão end in ão, which is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone marks both the nasal sound and the stress: NÃO, SÃO, VÃO are each one syllable. The circumflex of pôde is different from all of these: pode and pôde are both stressed on the first syllable, so the default rule needs no mark on either. The circumflex shows the closed o of pôde and exists to separate the two words.

Verbs ending in ar, er and ir (viajar, jogar, poder, dever, saber, chover, precisar) are stressed on the last syllable, which is the default for the ending r, so none of them needs an accent. Two vowels side by side: passear has two strong vowels, e and a, which never glide together, so it has three syllables, pas-se-AR. By contrast the ai of praia is a diphthong, PRAI-a.

Loanwords keep their foreign spelling. Shopping, as in shopping center, keeps sh, which is said as in English, and the final ng is not said as a consonant: it is said SHOH-pee, with the last vowel through the nose.

grammar.title: The near future: ir plus infinitive
grammar.explanation:
English builds its near future from the verb go: I am going to travel. Portuguese builds it the same way. It conjugates ir, to go, in the present and puts the main verb in the infinitive: eu vou viajar, literally I go to-travel. The two verbs have two jobs. A conjugated verb is one that changes its ending for person and number, and here that is ir: it says who is acting and that the action is ahead. The second verb stays in the infinitive, the dictionary form, and never changes: eu vou estudar, você vai estudar, nós vamos estudar, eles vão estudar. If you are tempted to change the second verb, stop: vou, vai, vamos and vão already carry the person. A verb that helps another verb in this way is called an auxiliary verb, and ir is the auxiliary here. English also has will, but everyday Brazilian Portuguese prefers ir plus infinitive for almost every future plan. The one-word future (falarei, I will speak) sounds formal or written, and it comes in a later unit.

Everything else follows the general rules from the lesson on how Portuguese works. The negative puts não directly before the conjugated verb, which is ir: eu não vou viajar, never eu vou não viajar. There is no helper like English do, so a question is the same words with rising intonation: você vai viajar? A question word goes first: o que você vai fazer amanhã? Fazer is to do or to make. To say that something will exist or happen, use ir with ter in its there-is sense (from the housing unit): vai ter chuva, vai ter festa, literally goes to-have rain, goes to-have party.

Time expressions go at the beginning or the end of the sentence: amanhã, hoje à noite (à is the crase of a plus a, since noite is feminine), no sábado, no fim de semana, semana que vem (next week, literally week that comes), mês que vem. Do not confuse the auxiliary with ir as an ordinary verb of motion. In eu vou à praia there is no second verb: ir is the main verb and a place follows, joined by the preposition a (à praia, ao cinema) or, informally, para (pra praia). With a verb the infinitive follows directly, with no preposition at all.

One point about sound. In fast speech vou is often said vô, but it is always written vou. The form vamos also has a second life as the invitation let's, which the last note of this unit covers.

grammar.title: Poder, querer, saber, precisar, dever
grammar.explanation:
These five verbs share one job: each adds an attitude to another verb, such as ability, wish, knowledge, need or duty. Verbs of this kind are called modal verbs. In English the modals can, must and should are special: they never take an -s for he or she, and they are followed by a bare verb with no to. Portuguese modals are ordinary verbs. They conjugate fully for person and number and are followed by an infinitive, so the structure is the one you just met with ir: the first verb carries the person and the second is an infinitive that never changes. Eu posso ir, nós podemos ir, eles podem ir. None of the five takes a preposition before the infinitive. Precisar takes de only before a noun.

Three of them are irregular in a way you can see. In poder the stem pod- becomes poss- in the eu form: posso. In querer the eu form is quero, and você quer loses its final -e. In saber the eu form sei does not resemble the stem at all. Everywhere else they follow the -er pattern you already know: podemos, queremos, sabemos, devemos for nós, and podem, querem, sabem, devem for vocês, eles and elas. Precisar and dever are fully regular. The spelling follows the sound rules: posso needs ss to keep the s sound between vowels, and quero and quer keep a silent u after q. Pode is said PÓ-jee because a d before the final e becomes j. A written pôde with a circumflex is a different word, the past form he could once, and its accent exists only to tell it from pode.

The meanings matter, because English can covers two ideas that Portuguese keeps apart. Poder is can in the sense that nothing stops you: possibility or permission, as in posso entrar?, may I come in? Saber is to know, and with an infinitive it means to know how to do something you have learned: eu sei nadar says I learned how to swim, while eu posso nadar says there is nothing to stop me swimming today. Querer is to want. Precisar is to need. Before a noun it takes de, which is literally to-need of: preciso de ajuda, and de fuses with the article as it always does (preciso do carro). Before an infinitive there is no de: preciso estudar. Dever literally means to owe: devo dinheiro, I owe money. The idea of a duty grew out of the idea of owing, so devo descansar means I ought to rest. It is milder than must.

In everyday speech Brazilians often use ter que for obligation: eu tenho que trabalhar amanhã, literally I-have that to-work. It sounds a little more insistent than precisar and sits close to English have to. For polite requests use pode: você pode repetir, por favor? And queria, which you met in the food unit, is a softer way to say I want.

grammar.title: Weather and seasons
grammar.explanation:
English weather sentences use the empty subject it with the verb to be: it is hot, it is raining. Portuguese has no word for it as a subject, so it uses verbs with no subject at all. A verb like this is called impersonal: it exists only in the third person singular, and no one performs it. Portuguese uses four structures for weather, and the weather word decides which.

First, fazer, literally to make, for temperature and sun: faz calor, faz frio, faz sol, literally makes heat, makes cold, makes sun. Calor and frio are nouns here, the thing that is made, so muito before them is an adjective and agrees with the noun, as in the housing unit: muito calor, muita chuva. Second, ter in its there-is sense, for what is present in the sky or the air: tem sol, tem vento, tem nuvens, literally has sun, has wind, has clouds. Faz sol and tem sol are both heard. Third, estar plus an adjective for how things are right now: está nublado, está quente (hot), está frio (frio is an adjective here, cold). With an adjective, muito is an adverb and does not change: está muito quente. In everyday speech people also say está calor and está frio, so faz calor and está calor are both normal. Quente is said KEN-chee: the u is silent, en is a nasal e, and t before the final e becomes ch.

Fourth, chover, to rain, is a weather verb in itself and exists only in the third person singular: chove means it rains, and vai chover means it is going to rain (the near future you just learned). Está chovendo uses a form you have not met: the gerund, a verb form ending in -ndo that says an action is in progress. You make it from the infinitive by changing -ar to -ando, -er to -endo and -ir to -indo: falar becomes falando and chover becomes chovendo. With estar it means is doing right now, as in English is raining. The full use of estar plus gerund belongs to a later unit, and here you only need it as a fixed way to say that it is raining. Brazilian Portuguese uses estar plus gerund; European Portuguese says está a chover.

To state a temperature use faz plus the number plus graus, degrees: faz trinta graus. The plural graus takes an s, and au is a diphthong said like ow. To ask about the weather say como está o tempo? or que tempo faz?, literally what weather makes?

The seasons are o verão, o outono, o inverno and a primavera. To say in a season, fuse em with the article: no verão, no outono, no inverno, na primavera. Brazil lies in the Southern Hemisphere, so its seasons are the reverse of those in North America and Europe: summer is roughly December to March and winter is June to September. Most of the country is tropical, so the real contrast is often between a rainy season and a dry season, and real cold is found mainly in the South and in some mountain regions.

grammar.title: Invitations: inviting, accepting and declining
grammar.explanation:
An invitation is not a separate piece of grammar. Portuguese builds invitations from verbs you already have, and the choice among them is about how directly you ask. The most natural invitation is vamos plus a place or an infinitive: vamos à praia? vamos jogar futebol? Vamos is the nós form of ir, so it literally says we go. With rising intonation it becomes a suggestion, much as English let's, short for let us, turns a statement into a proposal that includes the speaker. The same word is also the near future of the first note: nós vamos jogar futebol states a fact, we are going to play, while vamos jogar futebol? proposes it, and tone and context tell them apart. With a place, the preposition a fuses with the article: vamos ao cinema, vamos à praia (a plus o, a plus a). Informally you also hear vamos no cinema and vamos na praia.

Que tal means how about. Que is what and tal is such, so que tal um churrasco? is literally what such a barbecue? It takes a noun or an infinitive, not a conjugated verb: que tal um filme? que tal viajar? The direct question você quer ir...? asks about the person's wish, and the informal você topa? asks whether they are game. Topar means to accept or go along with a plan, and its older sense is to bump into something.

Accepting is short and warm: claro, com certeza (with certainty), boa ideia (good idea), topo (I'm up for it) and combinado. Combinado is the -ado form of combinar, to arrange or agree. It works like an adjective and means agreed, as in English it's agreed. Brazilians confirm with combinado or fechado (closed, as in a closed deal). To fix a time, ask a que horas?, literally at what hours? In quick speech people drop the a and say que horas? To fix a place, ask onde? For arrangements people say a gente se encontra no ponto às oito: the-people self finds at the stop at-the eight. The small word se is the same one you met in reflexive verbs, and with encontrar it means each other, so the sentence means we will meet. Por volta de, literally by turn of, means around: por volta das sete.

Declining is the delicate part. A bare não can sound abrupt in Brazil, so the usual shape has three steps: first a statement of inability with poder (hoje não posso), then the reason (preciso trabalhar), then regret (que pena) and often an alternative (e amanhã?). Choosing não posso, I can't, over não quero, I don't want to, is deliberate: it presents the refusal as a circumstance, not as a choice. Another courteous way to defer is fica para outra vez, literally it stays for another time, meaning let's do it another time.

culture.title: Weekends, weather and plans
culture.text:
Weekends in Brazil often revolve around friends and family. The classic plan is a churrasco, a barbecue with grilled meat, farofa and cold drinks, usually on Sunday at someone's house. Soccer is everywhere: people play a casual game called pelada with friends, and watch their favorite team on TV. In coastal cities the praia is a weekend habit, and in Rio de Janeiro you will see people on the sand all year long.

Because Brazil is in the Southern Hemisphere, summer is from December to March and winter is from June to September. Most of the country is warm all year, but the South can be cold, with frost and even snow on a few mountain days in July. The hot, rainy season in much of the country is the summer, when heavy afternoon storms are common. Carnaval happens in February or early March, in the hottest months, and festas juninas take place in June, in winter.

When Brazilians say vamos marcar (literally let's mark) or a gente combina (literally the people arranges), it does not always mean that a plan is fixed. If you want to be sure, propose a day and a time and wait for a combinado. Declining an invitation is normal, but it is friendlier to give a reason and suggest another day.

exercises.explanation: The conjugated verb is ir, in its eu form. The second verb, viajar, stays in the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the negative of 'Eu vou viajar', I am going to travel?
exercises.explanation: Não goes directly before the conjugated verb, which is vou. The infinitive viajar is not the verb that is negated.

exercises.prompt_en: What are you going to do tomorrow?
exercises.explanation: The question word comes first, then ir agrees with você (vai), then the infinitive.

exercises.hint_en: We are going to play soccer on Saturday.
exercises.explanation: Ir agrees with the subject nós: vamos. Jogar stays in the infinitive.

exercises.hint_en: Tomorrow it is going to be hot.

exercises.prompt: How is the final l of futebol said?
choices: Like the l of English light
Like w, as at the end of English now
exercises.explanation: An l at the end of a syllable is said w, so futebol ends in the w glide of now. Since the word ends in l, the stress is on the last syllable and no accent is needed.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about 'Faz calor' is true?
choices: It has no subject, because faz is an impersonal weather verb.
Its subject is ele, which was dropped.
Faz is a form of estar.
exercises.explanation: Faz is a form of fazer, to make. The sentence is literally makes heat. Nobody performs the verb, so there is no subject, and calor is only the thing that is made.

exercises.hint_en: Today it is cold in São Paulo.
exercises.explanation: Fazer (faz frio, makes cold) and estar (está frio, is cold) are both normal for temperature.
Estar plus the gerund (the -ndo form) says that an action is in progress right now. Chovendo is the gerund of chover.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says that it is raining at this moment?
exercises.explanation: Vai chover is about the future and chove describes a habit. Estar plus the gerund describes what is happening now.
Faz calor and está calor are both used. With the adjective quente, only estar is possible.
Brazil is in the Southern Hemisphere, so its seasons are the reverse of those in North America and Europe.

exercises.prompt_pt: Hoje eu não ___ ir à festa.

exercises.explanation: Saber with an infinitive means to know how to do something learned. The eu form is sei.

exercises.prompt: Ana never learned to swim. Which sentence describes her?
exercises.explanation: Saber is knowledge of a learned skill. Pode would say that something prevents her today, quer would say that she does not want to, and deve would say that she should not.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct for 'I need help'?
exercises.explanation: Precisar is literally to-need of, so it takes de before a noun. Before an infinitive, as in preciso estudar, there is no de.
Precisar followed by an infinitive takes no de.
Precisar takes de before a noun, and de fuses with the article o: de plus o gives do.

exercises.prompt_en: We are going to play soccer on Saturday.

choices: I don't want to today, sorry.

exercises.explanation: Before a noun, muito is an adjective and agrees with it. Chuva is feminine, so muita.

exercises.prompt: How is the d of verdade said, in ver-DA-de?

exercises.explanation: A d before the sound i becomes j. The final e is weak and said i, so the d of de is said like j: ver-DA-jee.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with the reason for its accent or the lack of one

pairs.en: a stressed open diphthong at the end of a word takes the acute
stressed on the third to last syllable, so an accent is always written
stressed on the second to last syllable, which the ending a predicts, so no accent
the tilde nasalizes the vowel and also marks the stress
stressed on the last syllable of a word ending in e, so an accent is needed

exercises.explanation: An accent appears when a word breaks the default stress of its ending, or in the special cases of open diphthongs and the third to last syllable.

exercises.prompt: Why does comédia carry an accent while academia does not?
choices: Comédia is stressed on the third to last syllable, co-MÉ-di-a, which no ending predicts. Academia is stressed on the second to last, a-ca-de-MI-a, which the ending a predicts.
Comédia is a verb and academia is a noun.
Accents are written only on words of foreign origin.
Academia ends in a consonant, so it needs no accent.
exercises.explanation: The ending ia counts as two syllables, so the stress of comédia falls on the third to last. Academia follows the default for a word ending in a.

exercises.prompt: Why is it ao in 'Vamos ao cinema?' but à in 'Vamos à praia?'
choices: Praia is plural, so it needs the accent.
The accent shows which syllable is stressed.
À is used before beaches and ao before every other place.
Cinema is masculine, so a plus o gives ao. Praia is feminine, so a plus a gives à.
exercises.explanation: The preposition a fuses with the article. The grave accent on à records the fusion of two a sounds and does not mark stress.

exercises.hint_en: I go to the gym in the morning.
exercises.explanation: Academia is feminine, so a plus a fuses into à. In casual speech na, pra and para a are also heard.

exercises.prompt_en: Do you want to go to the beach?
exercises.explanation: Querer is followed directly by the infinitive ir, and the place takes à.

exercises.prompt: In 'Vamos à praia?', what is the role of vamos?
choices: The nós form of ir, said with rising intonation as a suggestion: let's
A command addressed to one person
exercises.explanation: Vamos literally says we go. Said as a question it works as a proposal, and the same form is also the near future when it states a fact.

exercises.prompt: Match each Portuguese phrase with its literal, word-for-word meaning
exercises.explanation: The literal meaning shows how Portuguese builds the idea. The natural English translation is different: it is hot, it is sunny, it is going to rain, shall we go to the beach, definitely, let's do it another time.
Ir plus the infinitive chover. Vai ter chuva, literally goes to-have rain, is also natural.
Precisar takes an infinitive with no de. Tenho que is the colloquial alternative.

exercises.prompt: Which reply is the most natural way to decline an invitation to the beach?

exercises.explanation: The usual shape is a statement of inability with poder, a reason and a sign of regret. Não posso presents the refusal as a circumstance and não quero as a choice.

exercises.prompt: Why is lá, there, written with an accent?
choices: It is a stressed word of one syllable ending in a, and such words always take the acute.
It is stressed on the third to last syllable.
It is a fusion of the preposition a and the article a.
The accent shows that the a is nasal.
exercises.explanation: A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o (with or without s) takes an accent, as in já, pé, só, mês and nós. The grave of à is a different mark with a different job, and the tilde is the nasal mark.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct for 'How about traveling in July?'

exercises.prompt: Why does pôde carry a circumflex while pode does not?
choices: Pôde is stressed on the last syllable.
The circumflex marks a nasal vowel.
Both are stressed on the first syllable and need no mark by the default rule; the circumflex is a differential accent that separates the two words.
exercises.explanation: An accent that only tells two words apart is called a differential accent. Pode is he can and pôde is he could, on one occasion.

exercises.prompt_pt: Hoje ___ sol e amanhã vai chover.

exercises.prompt: Why can Portuguese say 'Nós vamos jogar' with jogar unchanged, while 'Nós jogamos' changes the ending?
choices: In the first, only vamos carries the person and number, so the second verb stays in the infinitive. In the second, jogar is the only verb and must carry them.
The first is informal and the second is formal.
